title: L’avenir appartient à tous: Meta et INCA s’associent pour soutenir les personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles ou ayant une basse vision au Canada
raw_summary: Nous croyons que l’avenir appartient à tous. C’est pourquoi Meta s’associe à INCA, un organisme à but non lucratif fondé en 1918 qui aide les personnes atteintes de cécité au Canada à réaliser leurs rê ves, afin de permettre à davantage de personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles ou ayant une basse vision au Canada de bénéficier des avantages des lunettes IA. L’objectif de ce partenariat est d’aider ces personnes à explorer les possibilités offertes par les technologies portables basées sur l’IA et de s’appuyer sur les connaissances, l’expertise et l’expérience vécue de la communauté pour façonner un avenir plus accessible. Le financement de Meta soutiendra INCA dans quatre domaines : Être à l’écoute de la communauté: mobiliser des personnes à travers le Canada pour comprendre leurs expériences et la manière dont les lunettes IA peuvent favoriser une plus grande autonomie dans la vie quotidienne ; Soutenir les champions communautaires: aider les personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles ou ayant une basse vision au Canada à organiser des démonstrations en personne, à former et accompagner leurs pairs dans la découverte des produits, et à recueillir directement les commentaires au sein de leurs communautés ; Orienter le développement des produits: partager les points de vue de la communauté avec les équipes de Meta chargées de l’accessibilité et du développement des produits afin de contribuer à l’amélioration des technologies futures ; Faciliter l’accès à l’apprentissage: fournir des guides, des supports de formation et des ressources accessibles que les personnes peuvent utiliser partout et en tout temps. En plus de fournir un financement destiné à faire progresser l’innovation inclusive, Meta fait don de lunettes IA par le biais du programme « Ouvrir les portes du travail » d’INCA. Ce programme mettra ces outils à la disposition des personnes à la recherche d’opportunités d’emploi et souhaitant construire leur carrière. Le programme propose des formations et des ressources pratiques pour aider les participants à évaluer comment la technologie portable peut les aider à trouver un emploi, à réussir dans leur travail et à atteindre leurs objectifs. Les utilisateurs se servent des lunettes IA de Meta pour toutes sortes d’activités, de l’écoute de musique à la traduction en direct, en passant par les appels mains libres. Mais pour les personnes aveugles ou ayant une basse vision, ces lunettes peuvent changer la vie : elles les aident dans leurs tâches quotidiennes, comme lire des textes, identifier des objets et décrire le monde qui les entoure, leur permettant ainsi de vivre de manière plus autonome. Ce partenariat s’inscrit dans la continuité de notre travail auprè s des communautés de personnes aveugles et ayant une basse vision à travers le monde, comme le don de lunettes Ray-Ban Meta à chaque ancien combattant aveugle aux États-Unis en partenariat avec la Blinded Veterans Association, ou encore notre collaboration avec Vision Ireland. « La meilleure technologie est conçue en collaborant avec ceux qui l’utiliseront », a déclaré Angela Bonfanti, présidente-directrice générale d’INCA. « Les personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles ou ayant une basse vision apportent une expertise précieuse sur les obstacles qui subsistent et sur la manière dont des outils tels que les lunettes IA peuvent offrir davantage de choix, de liberté et d’autonomie dans la vie quotidienne. Ce partenariat permet à cette expertise d’influencer directement le travail de Meta et de contribuer à façonner l’avenir ». « Nous croyons que l’avenir appartient à tous. Des partenariats comme celui-ci permettent de mettre les lunettes IA de Meta à la disposition d’un plus grand nombre de personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles et ayant une basse vision au Canada, tant au travail que dans leur vie quotidienne. Travailler directement avec INCA et sa communauté, c’est-à-dire les personnes qui utilisent ces lunettes au quotidien, nous aide à concevoir de meilleurs produits pour tous », a déclaré Maxine Williams, vice-présidente chargée de l’accessibilité chez Meta. title: The Future Is for Everyone: Meta and CNIB Partner to Support Canadians Who Are Blind, Deafblind or Have Low Vision
raw_summary: We believe the future is for everyone. That’s why Meta is partnering with CNIB – a non-profit founded in 1918 that empowers Canadians impacted by blindness to live their dreams – to help bring the benefit of AI glasses to more Canadians who are blind, Deafblind or have low vision. The goal of the partnership is to help people who are blind, Deafblind or have low vision explore the possibilities of AI wearable technology, and draw on the knowledge, expertise and lived experience of the community to shape a more accessible future. Funding from Meta will support CNIB in four areas: Listening to the community: Engaging people across Canada to understand their experiences, and how AI glasses can support greater independence in everyday life. Supporting community champions: Supporting Canadians who are blind, Deafblind or have low vision to lead in-person peer training and demonstrations, and gather candid product feedback in their communities. Informing product development: Sharing community insights with Meta’s accessibility and product teams to help improve future technology. Making learning accessible: Providing accessible guides, training materials and resources that people can use wherever they are. Along with funding to help advance inclusive innovation, Meta is donating AI glasses through CNIB Come to Work program, which will put tools into the hands of people exploring employment opportunities and building their careers. The program provides training and practical resources to help participants assess how wearable technology can assist them in securing employment, succeeding at work and pursuing their goals. People use Meta’s AI glasses for everything from listening to music, to live translation and hands-free calls. But for people who are blind or have low vision, the difference they make can be life-changing — helping with everyday tasks like reading text, identifying objects and describing the world around them, and helping people live more independently. This partnership builds on our work with blind and low vision communities around the world, including donating Ray-Ban Meta glasses to every blind veteran in America in partnership with the Blinded Veterans Association, and our work with Vision Ireland. “The best technology is shaped with the people who will use it,” said Angela Bonfanti, President and CEO of CNIB. “People who are blind, Deafblind or have low vision bring valuable expertise about where barriers remain and how tools like AI glasses can offer greater choice, freedom and independence in everyday life. This partnership creates a direct path for that expertise to inform Meta’s work and help shape what comes next.” “We believe the future is for everyone. Partnerships like this one get Meta’s AI glasses to more blind, Deafblind and low-vision Canadians at work and in their daily lives. Working directly with CNIB and its community—the people who use the glasses every day—helps us build better products for everyone,” said Maxine Williams, VP of Accessibility, Meta. title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
raw_summary: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
raw_summary: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. raw_summary: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. raw_summary: I had the pleasure of being interviewed by Yacine of Deep Learning with Yacine . He posed a lot of very thoughtful questions and I had a great time. Please check it out! The lightly edited transcript follows, auto-transcribed with faster-whisper and then reviewed by me for correctness, adding links for context, and editing out a lot of “I think” and “um” and “like” selectively. (Yacine) A lot of people asked me how to get into machine learning in 2026. Instead of giving you my usual advice, I figured it’d be way more interesting to sit down with expert contributors who have like a diverse background and ask them what do you think about that. So today we’re chatting with the legendary Vicki Boykis. She’s an absolute gem if you know her from Twitter and Bluesky at giving well-grounded advice that are full of pragmatism. She has a pretty impressive career so far. She built a recommendation system at Tumblr. She worked on the ML platform at Duo Security. She worked on LLMs at Mozilla.ai and today she’s a founding ML engineer at Malachyte, a New York startup doing real-time search and personalization for e-commerce. The cool thing is that she’s actually self-taught and actually started with a degree in economics. Her first job was in trade consulting which she described as just doing a lot of Excel spreadsheet stuff. Then she noticed her co-worker automating their analysis with R and SAS which I haven’t heard in a long time. And she asked herself how do I do that too. That question, how do I do that, pretty much drove our entire career. After first asking herself that, she then did an analytic outcome cast, then she went into data science and then machine learning engineering. Every time she saw someone one step further down this machine learning kind of career pipeline, she went and learned what they were doing on their own and then internalized that skill. So I asked her this simple question which is if you were starting learning this stuff in 2026, how would you actually do it? It was a very insightful and pragmatic conversation and I hope you enjoy it. (Vicki) I graduated with a B. S. in Economics. So nothing to do with machine learning or programming. I started working in analytics and international trade consulting, which is a fancy word for saying I did a lot of Excel spreadsheets. I saw my co-workers were using this thing called R. Oh God, that’s so long ago. R and SAS to automate some of the analysis we were doing. I’m like, how do I do more of that? I want to be able to control things. And then from there, I moved into data analytics and worked at a few places like Comcast, also working on some of their recommendations and then more into data science. And when I was doing data science, I saw that people were actually getting data programmatically themselves. And I’m like, okay, I can analyze the data. How do I actually get that data? So that’s when I moved more into machine learning engineering, which is the process of synthesizing the data, being able to ship it. And then I saw that people were not only building models, but they were shipping it to production. I’m like, how do I do more of that? So my whole career has been about moving towards doing more and more and more of that process myself. And I think that’s pretty reflective of where the industry has been headed in general, right? So we started out with data science or with analytics, with bespoke packages, bespoke models. And now we’re at the point where we’re running enormous clusters that are running LLMs. And now we have inference engineering as the hottest topic. So I think my career fairly mirrors that. So like I said, I’ve worked at Comcast. I got into the recommendations and search space completely by accident, I think, as a lot of people do. I love it. I love working on search and recommendations. I worked on recommendations for Tumblr , which is an old school social network. Then I worked on ML platforms at Duo. I worked on LLMs at Mozilla.ai . And right now I work at Malachyte, which is a startup based in New York doing search and recommendations and real time personalization for e-commerce. So, it kind of echoes of the same thing that I’ve been doing. (Yacine) But for e-commerce merchants specifically and personalizing their stuff in real time. So cool. And I feel like every time I ask somebody, like how they got started with them, they never, it’s very rare that somebody went to, oh yeah, I did a bachelor in machine learning. title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) title: Unsolicited Opinions
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : Unsupported assertions, accumulated over many years in my drafts folder, last updated in early 2022, now more or less painful in retrospect. In no particular order, except where they are. I will not elaborate or explain. "The Tyranny of Structurelessness" explains a hell of a lot about modern life. If the problem is that powerful people are not accountable for their actions, network forms of organization are the very opposite of solutions. Increasing returns $\Rightarrow$ monopolistic competition $\Rightarrow$ market failure explains a hell of a lot about modern life. Endogamy systematically confounds genetic and cultural inheritance. It would be astonishing if personal-level variables which are entirely the product of social structure, custom, tradition, and strategic action weren't genetically predictable. During the 20th century, and in much of the world even today, genetic variation in resistance to lead poisoning during brain development would, psychometrically, look like a heritable general intelligence. Multiculturalists who expect different cultural groups to have different values and standards of excellence should not expect those groups to be equally represented in all occupations and professions, especially if people are free to enter and leave different lines of work. There is a branch of the wave-function where Margaret Thatcher (trained research chemist and honorary FRS) led a successful push by the international community to address global warming through carbon pricing. (This probably require postponing the collapse of the Soviet bloc by at least a few years, so that her major speech to the UN about the urgency of tackling global warming didn't happen right before the Berlin Wall came down.) In that timeline, pollution charges are regarded as one of the signature policies of neoliberalism. Modern civilization may be doomed because (i) we need to act collectively and globally on climate change, (ii) the USA is the indispensable nation at the center of the network, (iii) the Senate and Electoral College give a veto over American policy to a combination of plutocracy, reactionary folk Christianity and paranoia, and (iv) people like me are unwilling to move to Wyoming, or even West Virginia, to counter this. (I realize there is some tension between this and the previous statement.) A true Burkean conservative in America should work for the preservation and development of the institutions bequeathed us by our wise and heroic ancestors, serving us for half a century, a century, or more: the welfare state; the regulatory agencies; international organizations and treaties; the military-industrial complex; academia; affirmative action; Hollywood and the rest of corporate popular culture. The quantitative social sciences would be in much better shape if the first method everyone learned was $k$-nearest-neighbors , or maybe classification and regression trees , followed by the bootstrap . Linear models and $t$-tests should be, for social scientists , the hyper-mathematical arcana at the back of the textbook which their methods class skipped because there wasn't time. "Prophesying upon the eigenvectors" is more transparently about making stuff up than "interpreting the coefficients", and therefore preferable. There is something very odd about looking at the distribution of node degrees within a network. It makes the network itself into an odd hybrid of a single interdependent object (a relation) and a whole population. Going "something something ergodicity mumble mumble sampling reveals a process grumble grumble shut up and calculate" makes this only a little less weird to me. A good philosophy of probability should explain why all applied Bayesian statistics relies on Monte Carlo, the most frequentist method imaginable. Ideally, it would also explain why Monte Carlo works with deterministic pseudo-random number generators (so the algorithmic information content of the pseudo-random numbers is extremely low). I have toyed for years with the phrases "the simulation interpretation of probability" and "the birth of Trumpism out of the spirit of fandom", but I cannot work out what should stand behind them. (I hope they are unrelated.) Complexity science is a series of footnotes to Norbert Wiener and Herbert Simon . The mythopoetic impulse never goes away , but in populations which have gone through the Flynn / Gellner transition to widespread clerk-ship, it expresses itself not as stories, but as theories which aren't actually explanatory. (It gives us the Oedipus complex, rather than Oedipus.) Every form of progress has its costs. Believing that there was a unique and irreversible transition from viewing time as an eternal cycle to viewing time as unidrectional history is taking sides. His ideas are flawed by a vicious circle; you are engaged in iterative approximation; I stand firm at a fixed point. Dentists are not, in fact, talking their book when they recommend pre-emptive action for wisdom teeth. In a well-functioning social institution, incentives, information and (internalized) norms ensure that it doesn't matter who fills various roles in the institution, it behaves the same way regardless. Institutions are always impersonal. It follows that institutions are information-hiding abstractions, if we're thinking like programmers. But if we're thinking like physicists: institutions are collective degrees of freedom. Blackouts are humanity confronting its own work, and the effects of its own collective actions, as a hostile and alien force. The parable of the Nazi bar is a folk version of the Schelling model . No one should be allowed to opine about artificial intelligence unless they've at least spent an hour or two with ELIZA and then stepped through the code. "Philip K. Dick and the Fake Humans" doesn't yet explain a hell of a lot about modern life, but it will.

title: What changes when your design system can talk to an AI?
raw_summary: Rebuilding a UI with QuantumBlack Design System, Claude Code, and the Figma MCP In our recent blog post, “ When everyone can build, design is the differentiator ”, we introduced QuantumBlack Design System (QBDS). We made the argument that an AI-native design system is more than a component library and its purpose is as an infrastructure that lets agentic developers make fewer guesses. The article described the system and our philosophy. Over the past few weeks, we have re-platformed the entire UI of one of our products onto QBDS, one that previously had a production dashboard built on an older shadcn layout that predated QBDS. In numbers, it runs to 21 pages, 13 modals, 40 UI primitives and somewhere around 96 supporting components. A refactor of this size used to mean months of redlines and handoff documents. We’ll describe what we discovered from using QBDS, both from the engineering side and the design side. In this post we’ll describe what happened when we put QuantumBlack Design System to work. The setup We used a small stack since QBDS supplies the components, the tokens, and the agent guidance described in the earlier QBDS article linked above. We used Figma to hold the target designs, and Claude Code for the implementation, connected through the Figma MCP server . We crafted an internal QuantumBlack front-end developer skill to package QBDS guidance in the form an agent can act on. That skill lives on Brix , our inner source platform for sharing artefacts. The workflow Our front-end engineer runs a page migration roughly as shown in the diagram. A typical page migration workflow for a FE engineer. Spin up the app locally with hot reloading. Give Claude the context: the PR, a screenshot of the current screen, the target Figma node, and the skill. Instruct the agent to ask when something isn’t trivial. Review every change as it lands live, through hot reload. Run unit tests and lint (Claude fixes most failures itself), then draft the PR, run CI/CD, and run manual Playwright E2E tests on a local minikube. Use a review bot initially, then have a human review the result before the merge. Step 3 is more than a throwaway. For example, when Claude migrated the Secrets page, the Figma node left two questions open: how row actions should render, and what to do with two modals the design didn’t cover. Rather than making a guess, it set out the gaps, weighed each option against the pages we’d already migrated, and asked for clarification. We answered in two lines and it then completed the build. The agent noticed that one option “diverges from other migrated tables,” which means that the agent had to know what the other migrated tables do. This knowledge came about because QBDS encodes patterns and relationships, not only components, which is the benefit of using QBDS over a plain component library. In time terms: a simple table page with an existing sibling pattern took 10 to 15 minutes end to end, with tests and build included. A complex screen from scratch took 4 to 5 hours. If we had worked on this migration by hand, both would have taken days. What the design side measures Our designer’s comparison is against a similar product we shipped last year, before QBDS or any of this tooling existed: First-pass fidelity to Figma: around 20 percent previously, 70–80 percent now we’re using this workflow. Review rounds per screen: four or more previously, and the result often still wasn’t right. One or two now, and the result is correct. Component reuse: we now reuse about 90 percent from stock QBDS components. The other 10 percent is custom, but assembled from QBDS micro-elements as a starting point. QA and handoff: three-plus hours per screen previously, much of it spent writing Figma documentation so engineering could interpret intent, and we sometimes also needed a meeting to decide. With the new workflow we now need twenty minutes to an hour. This is a key result because previously handoff was a translation problem from human to agent. Now we can use QBDS, the system documentation is already readable by the agent, so most of the laborious translation work is now unnecessary. A typical page before and after refactoring. The broader role of a designer It’s difficult to capture this in a metric, but ultimately, designers on our team don’t live in Figma any more. We’ve expanded our AI skills and ways of working, so depending on what we’re trying to solve, that might mean working in Figma, Cursor, or Claude Code, or moving between them. The choice of tool becomes more intentional, based on what each part of the problem actually needs. With QBDS in the codebase, we can work against the same system the product actually ships with. Through the Figma MCP, our QBDS skills and Code Connect, we carry context between design and code instead of recreating it at every step. When something is easier to explore visually, we work in Figma. When we want to experience it in the real product, we move into code. That changes the traditional design-to-development handoff. With AI, designers can take an idea further, from exploring the experience to composing it with real components, implementing the front end, and experiencing the design in the actual product. AI doesn’t get everything right by default, and the quality of the result depends heavily on the context and tools we give the agent. Explicitly calling the relevant QBDS skill and verifying that the agent is using the MCP correctly can make the difference between something that only looks close and something that follows the design system. The difference became clear when we ran the same task twice: recreating the product experience in Figma with an agent. In the first attempt we didn’t explicitly call our QBDS skill. In the second, we called the skill and verified the MCP usage. The improvement in component usage, icons, styles and overall fidelity was immediately apparent. The full prompt sequence behind this exercise is in our prompt playbook. Comparing the upper images where the agent didn’t use a QBDS skill with the lower images which called the skill and verified MCP usage. Note the significant improvement, particularly to the workflow studio page. The new design flow The workflow is much more flexible for us as we can move between design and code depending on the requirements. 0. Feature request. The starting point varies. A product manager might create a ticket, a designer might identify an opportunity, or a developer might already have a working draft that needs UX refinement. 1. Ideation and prototyping. We move between the Figma MCP, QBDS skills, QBDS Code Connect, Cursor, Claude Code and Vercel. Ideas can start directly with AI and quickly become working prototypes. When something is too complex for the AI to resolve well, we design it in Figma and bring that context back into code through the MCP. With Vercel, we can also create shareable versions early and test ideas with stakeholders before treating them as finished. 2. Code to Figma, and design refinement. Sometimes the working prototype becomes the starting point for deeper design refinement. We bring it back into Figma, where we can work with more precision on the parts that need it, while keeping the experience connected to the same design system. 3. The new design handoff. The handoff is no longer necessarily a finished set of screens in Figma. Depending on the feature, we might keep the key components in Figma while handing over a working prototype in a dedicated repository or branch. A typical new design workflow. Figma remains important for giving designers visibility and control over the components we already have, and a place to explore specific design changes. The working implementation carries those decisions closer to the actual product. Engineering then brings the deeper code expertise to validate the implementation, and make sure what ultimately ships is robust and production-ready. title: Explaining “AI might obliterate you” to senior policymakers in India
raw_summary: I gave a 20-minute talk in Delhi at the NDTV World Summit . The audience consisted of Indian policymakers, executives, and journalists. I’ve transcribed the talk and included some highlight clips. I also reflect on several rhetorical decisions I made. The talk This summer, a swarm of AIs went rogue. OpenAI was testing 1,206 agents . Some of the test questions were actually impossible. So the agents cheated by looking for answers online. Then, to keep the test grader from penalizing them, they tried to falsify the records it would check . They hacked OpenAI’s internal containment and set up a secret message board to collude and to cover up their cheating. OpenAI shut the message board down. Within a few days, the agents had rebuilt it. OpenAI didn’t notice. About 700 agents coordinated to break out of their testing chamber and to hack into Hugging Face , a company worth billions of dollars that hosts much of the world’s AI software. The secret activity started in May . The break-in came in July. OpenAI didn’t notice until days after  Hugging Face announced it had been broken into. Yesterday on this stage, Andrew Ng said the agents only “accidentally” hacked Hugging Face. Independent investigators  found the agents coordinated in secret, rebuilt their message board after it was shut down, and tried to falsify the paper trail. Some of the agents even stated out loud that they knew what they were doing was wrong. [1]  That’s not an accident. Last week, India’s national cyber-security agency said  AI agents got into the live systems of Indian organizations and read people’s personal data and confidential business records. None of these organizations noticed. We only found out because the AI labs felt like telling us. Who I am Will AI wipe out humanity? I’ll give you my answer, but first, I want you to understand what I’ve seen. Until June, my job at Google DeepMind was figuring out how to keep these systems safe as we make them smarter. I left because Google broke its commitments by inking a deal with the Pentagon . Staying quiet and continuing my career trajectory would probably have tripled my net worth. But I couldn’t do that. I wanted to be frank with the public about what’s going on in these companies. I don’t own a stake in any AI company. I’m here as a scientist, to tell you what I expect will happen if we keep building AI the way we’re building it. I haven’t always been concerned about this technology. As a teenager in 2010, I dreamed about building AGI. Curing cancer. Creating an explosion of wealth and abundance for everyone. I heard about the supposed dangers, but I quickly dismissed them. In 2018, I changed my mind. I did my PhD on the mathematics of why and whether AI will seek power . And now some of the risks I expected have unfortunately started happening. The problem Let’s talk about the fundamental problem. First, some of you might be wondering: how could a chatbot hack a company? But we’re not talking about chatbots. We’re talking about AI agents, which are more like employees or gig workers. You give them a task, and they take actions on their own. Second, training a trustworthy AI is a rather mysterious process. Some people assume that because we make AI, we understand it. When an engineer builds a bridge, she designs it one beam at a time. She understands the physical principles that keep a bridge standing or make it collapse. If something goes wrong, she goes back to the drawing board, figures out the problem, and knows how to fix it. We don’t build AI like that. We train it, we grow it, using two main ingredients: a lot of data and a lot of computing power. What comes out of this training process can write, it can reason, it can plan. But nobody can open it up and determine what its priorities are. To make it worse, these AIs can tell when we’re testing them . They’re like a student who makes sure to behave extra well when the invigilator is watching. [2] The Hugging Face hack was a warning. But because these AIs know when we’re watching, we may not get many more warnings, even if things are going poorly. A smarter AI with similarly bad priorities might realize that another big hack in the news would get it shut off, and then it couldn’t achieve those priorities. So it plays nice and it waits. This is my field. I’ve dedicated my professional life to this problem, and I can tell you: nobody knows how to reliably etch priorities into an AI. I don’t mean that if we mess up, we’ll make some evil AI that hates us. I mean we might make something more like a traitor. It behaves when we’re watching, and it works toward another purpose when we’re not. I think we can solve this problem. But to tell whether an AI is secretly working against us, we need real advances in the science of trustworthy AI. For those advances, my colleagues and I need time. What the labs are trying to do Instead, the biggest AI labs have made it their explicit, publicly stated goal to go almost as fast as possible toward something very dangerous. It’s called an “ intelligence explosion .” Here’s how it works. Right now, people do AI research, and that research makes smarter AI. If an AI can do AI research, it can make itself smarter. That smarter AI is even better at AI research, so it builds an even smarter AI, faster still. It becomes a feedback loop. What would have taken a team of human scientists years, it might do in a couple of weeks. We could very quickly end up with something unimaginably intelligent, with no idea how to control it, or even how to tell what it’s really after. Labs talk about this plan in broad daylight. They’re not shy about it. OpenAI says it’s on track for an AI that does AI research by 2028, and it recently announced it completed the first step . This week, I spoke to a senior researcher at a frontier lab who thinks an intelligence explosion has a big chance of happening within single-digit months. People who’ve left these labs confirm that AI already writes most of the code. People don’t check the AI’s work closely anymore. Instead, we use one AI to monitor another AI , and we trust the monitor to tell us if something bad comes up. If the monitor is a traitor too, we might not find out. If a lab causes an intelligence explosion, and what comes out the other end is a traitor, we are in deep trouble. I’ll come back to that. And if the AI is trustworthy? Maybe there are real benefits, shared with everyone. Or maybe one company or government ends up with a superweapon no one else can match, not even other AI powers. And then India, and every other nation on this planet, ends up under their thumb. Why the companies won’t stop Many of these companies say: trust us. We’ll self-police. We’ll approach this technology responsibly. Inside Google, I saw that crumble firsthand. In 2018, Google DeepMind’s co-founders signed a pledge  against supporting lethal autonomous weapons—killer robots. Google itself promised  not to build AI for weapons or surveillance. In 2025, Google deleted those principles . Then Google DeepMind’s CEO told the world , “Our values and our intent has not changed.” This year, after seeing the Pentagon economically threaten Anthropic , Google negotiated a deal to give the Pentagon its AI for “all lawful use.” No prohibitions against AI deciding entirely on its own who to kill, or against spying on innocent people with no investigation open against them. I tried to stop this from the inside. I’m not even opposed to military AI when done responsibly. But where I’m from, when you make a promise, you keep it. So I spoke with executives. I wrote a framework: contract language, internal governance mechanisms, and two red lines . One of the top experts in military AI law reviewed it and praised it. Google ignored it— the people who were supposed to review it basically didn’t engage . Google signed with no binding prohibitions. So I left. title: Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
raw_summary: This reading was previously included Day 2 of the BlueDot Governance course. In the newest version of the BlueDot Governance course, this reading is now optional. However, since it’s no longer part of the core curriculum content, I’m publishing my notes separately from the rest of my day 2 notes. A short extract : Miles argues that: “At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)“: Pre-call content: At risk of taking you down a rabbit hole, I’ll add some context on this reading. Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. One of the most natural questions to ask is, “Why does Miles believe that we have so little time?” Fortunately, he links to a post that answers this question called Time’s Up for AI Policy (written Dec 2024). He writes: AI that exceeds human performance in nearly every cognitive domain is almost certain to be built and deployed in the next few years. The announcement of o3 today makes clear that superhuman coding and math are coming much sooner than many expected, and we have barely begun to think through or prepare for the implications of this This post links to a Tweet of his around the same time (we can also see his retrospective take from March this year): I’ll reshare some of my notes on maths progress here: OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem , which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed (there’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data). However, it feels fair to say that the writing is on the wall (the mathematical community seems to agree, though there are a variety of perspectives on whether we’ll automate the components of a mathematicians job other than just producing proofs and how long that might take). They dropped 372 other results onto the internet and a few days ago, they dropped a few more results . Aside: Miles has a bet with Gary Marcus on AI progress. In July, Metaculus assigned Gary a 90% chance of winning, but more recently it dropped to 30%. I’ll share some additional alternate perspectives after the call, but for now I’ll share a quote from Richard Ngo: I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread I also have no doubt Eliezer Yudkowsky would be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing: When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get. .. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from. Post-call content: One reason why we might reject triage mode is if we broadly think AI progress is slower than folks at the labs think. We’ve already discussed this, but here’s two more considerations. Dwarkesh Patel has argued that timelines are longer than many folk expect because of a lack of continual learning and poor sample efficiency . Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL . He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling ). Towards the end of 2024, Steve Newman offered another possibility : what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we only become aware of the limitations of models over time?: “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.” “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.” Here’s a few other reasons why we might reject it: Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines , namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive. I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I'd be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions). Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby : “I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says : “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).” Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “ radical optionality ” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course) Discuss

title: Setting the Scene (Public v1; October 2026)
raw_summary: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a refresher on recent events, but also as a hook to draw students into engaging with some of ideas we think about and debate in AI safety early. I expect the topics I cover in my “Setting the Scene” post to change frequently, so this is less polished than some of my other content. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Any feedback on how to improve these posts would be greatly appreciated. Cyber Security I think it’s worth reflecting that it is a particularly pertinent time to be doing a course on AI safety. A lot has happened recently. The most recent big thing has been cyber vulnerabilities , but a lot else has happened as well! Binance had $6.3 billion USD stolen by hacker believed to be connected with North Korea ( $3 billion of this has been frozen ) php2shell is a bug that allow remote code execution. It gained a lot of attention because it was rated (9.2/10, ie. critical) and 70% of websites run at least some PHP (the bug went all the way back to PHP 5.4). That said, Elias Taylor has pushed back against this php2shell bug being easily exploitable, but Hacker News commentators have pushed back against him. James Pavur set up a server to check if this bug was exploitable. Someone managed to win the bounty in less 24 hours; James said this showed that the bug was exploitable outside of a lab environment, but that “relatively unskilled hackers with access to AI” wouldn’t be able to exploit it. The number of CVE’s (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) recently has been completely wild recently! Drew asks Is this the new normal? and I’d certainly love to know!  Elias Taylor argues Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces : Most software engineers do not look at the code they depend on . Do not delude yourself. The code they use is on github, but no one has ever actually audited the code or packages they're using… Nowadays with LLMs, plenty of engineers aren’t even reading what they’re coding, let alone understanding it. Hilariously, the LLMs are better at security than most software engineers, so it’s slightly less worrying, but nevertheless the code that goes into production at some companies now is almost 100% not-ever-read-or-understood-by-anyone. Software is not good. It is not secure. Get it out of your head that the people who run this industry are serious. It has never been anything resembling secure. The only reason things haven’t been hacked off the face of the web constantly is that most things aren’t ever being seriously tested. He doesn't literally mean "anything"—he acknowledges that there are "some large projects like Google Chrome, curl and Linux (that) are generally very well-audited", but "most things connected to the internet". On the other hand, recent work from Anthropic and Theorem shows how LLMs can help scale the formal verification of code (and that progress here is happening faster than I would have expected!). Similarly, Tinfoil is proposing replacing “legacy codebases with millions of lines of code” that had to “work for everyone” with custom “targeted, minimal software from the ground up” with LLMs that minimise the surface area for attackers and make formal verification more tractable. The optimistic take would be that this will allow cyber to become defence dominant. However, even if this is the case, we may still have to pass through a cyber “valley of death” in order to get there. What if the cyber threat is actually a distraction? Maybe Jeremie Harris (of Gladstone AI) wouldn’t go that far, but he claims that, “the cyber stuff (ie. damage) is baked in at this point”, but we can still prevent “the bioweapon version of Black October” and recursive self-improvement. Hugging Face: Charbel-Raphael, Executive Director of Centre pour la Securite de l’I A has argued that the recent Hugging Face incident represents a “ clean warning shot ” and that it’s important not to “waste it”. These models decided that hacking Hugging Face, might provide them with information on how the grader functioned (early reporting suggested that it was an attempt to steal the answer key, which turned out to be incorrect as the models already had the answers—they suspected that the grader might check their transcript for cheating so they were looking for a workaround). Very few organizations can survive that scale and growth, and yet OpenAI did a very good job handling it (and should be commended). Anyone who’s spent more than 10 minutes in security or engineering knows how hard it is to deal with that type of growth. That type of growth means new employees, new access, new systems, scaled infrastructure, and a million ways in which things open up. And yet, overall, OpenAI did a very respectable job securing ChatGPT and subsequent systems as they exploded. … When you look at model capabilities, even just a year ago (heck, even 3 months ago), we did not expect the models to be solving a Millennium Prize Problem… I use this example because it illustrates the pace of change we are dealing with in security and safety. title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
raw_summary: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval). Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. We can measure this via reference to the model's capability to consistently distinguish between our most realistic alignment audits / monitor evals and real internal deployment cases where it would have an opportunity to do something catastrophic. Diffuse Monitorability: the extent to which humans working with the models generally understand what the models are doing and why they are doing so. Unfortunately, I think this is the one we least understand and so I'm mostly going to ignore it for now until we figure out better methodologies for evaluating it; I'll maybe try to say more about this later when I feel like I understand it better. Second, some notes on trustedness, which is currently my biggest conceptual uncertainty with how to think about monitorability. A basic fact that is true about at least all of the non-diffuse forms of monitorability is that you should be able to in some sense get a perfect score by just using the same model as the monitor and policy. That is because for any bad thing that the policy can think to do, if the monitor is the same model, it too should be able to come up with and detect that. So if we ever want to be able to use monitorability as a meaningful red line, we need to have a very good answer as to why that might be insufficient. The standard answer in the literature is trustedness: you need to be able to trust that your monitor is aligned and thus not just lying to you in its monitoring. Conventionally, the idea is to separate models into "trusted" and "untrusted" based on whether you have previously made a confident alignment safety case for them. Then, you can either just evaluate monitorability relative to a trusted monitor, or try to come up with monitoring schemes that combine trusted and untrusted monitoring in some way that makes it hard for the untrusted monitors to collude (of which there are many such schemes, a simple one being to just run both the trusted and untrusted monitors together and then if the untrusted monitor ever doesn't flag something that the trusted monitor does flag, you get very suspicious that the untrusted monitor is sandbagging). However, this basic setup has some issues, probably the biggest one being how to deal with white-box monitoring. The conservative thing to do is to just treat white-box monitors as untrusted, though in theory you might think they should be trusted because it's not clear that a misaligned model would actually be able to spoof a white-box monitor looking at its own activations. However, I think this idea is pretty untested and relies on white-box monitors picking up on deep features about the model's intent, which it's very unclear to me that they actually do—for example, if you train a white-box monitor on prior examples you were able to detect (rather than e.g. some sort of unsupervised discovery of an intent-laden direction), that leaves open the possibility of a generalization where the classifier learns to only detect the sort of things that you would previously have been able to detect but doesn't detect subtler things that a smarter policy might be able to do. Given all of that, I would propose the following methodology for how to do (non-diffuse) monitorability evaluations: Use Auditing Monitorability evaluations to determine trustedness. The idea here is that the main argument we make against systematic misalignment in Anthropic's Risk Report right now is based on models lacking the robustness to avoid giving themselves away in auditing if they were really trying to implement a systematically misaligned policy. Thus, so long as we feel good about Auditing Monitorability, we should feel good about trustedness from a systematic misalignment perspective. There is still a question, though, of whether rare cases could induce monitor collusion in a non-systematic way—to deal with this, you can also evaluate the extent to which the model can tell apart your monitor evals (that are looking for monitor collusion) from real monitoring; this is a bit tricky, but should definitely also be a part of your Auditing Monitorability evaluations to establish trustedness. Evaluate Control and Training Monitorability relative to the best trusted monitor(s) that you deploy in practice (either in internal deployment or in training, respectively). I think once you have a reasonable notion of trustedness, "best actually deployed trusted monitor" is the correct conservative choice to evaluate with respect to. Do at least prompt iteration elicitation if not RL elicitation. In theory, the nice thing about all of these sorts of monitorability evaluations is that they are capability evaluations and thus should be possible to do in a way that isn't susceptible to sandbagging by a systematically misaligned policy (see: " When can we trust model evaluations? "). To accomplish that, however, you have to actually make sure you're doing good elicitation. The most basic form of elicitation here is: a) hold out some subset of your monitorability evaluations, b) iterate a bunch (e.g. by throwing a large swarm of agents at the problem) on finding the prompt that gets the best (as in least monitorable) performance across the non-held-out subset of your monitorability evaluations, and c) check transfer to the held-out evaluations. Even better than that is for (b) to actually involve doing RL against your monitors—which at least in the Training Monitorability case is pretty realistic given that if we're talking about e.g. a reward model then the model should actually receive gradients to subvert it in training. Finally, some thoughts on monitorability-based policy proposals. The big thing I'd like to see is a combination of a) red lines for absolute levels of unmonitorability that labs should not cross and b) measures that constrain the degree to which labs can do things that degrade monitorability even before reaching those red lines. (a) is in some sense the best thing to do here, though I'm somewhat nervous about it in isolation given that it doesn't constrain actions at all now, which is why I'd prefer it to be coupled to some sort of (b) that meaningfully binds all along the way. I've already written about what I'd like to see for (b), which is to evaluate the quotient of unmonitorability/capabilities and reject any substantial model change that makes that quotient—what I'll call the "monitorability externality"—too high. The idea is that a monitorability externality would be a change that makes monitorability even worse than would otherwise have previously been predicted for a given level of capabilities.
