title: Introducing Geist Serif
raw_summary: Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens. Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif . Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices. Same system, new voice At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu. A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar . From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print. Display first Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit , which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley. When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go. Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices. From the first prototype to today The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today. Geist grew teeth The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures. The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.” Four families, one x-height Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size. Metric Geist Sans Geist Serif UPM 1000 1000 Cap height 710 710 x-height 530 530 Ascender 710 750 Descender -150 -200 Four variants, one axis Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape ( ELSH ), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart. Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings : Crafted by hand In July the font had 227 glyphs . It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g , for example, is tilted exactly 7°. Specs at a glance Geist Serif ships with: 1 weight (Regular) 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart) 894 glyphs 5 stylistic sets ( ss01 to ss05 ) 352 supported languages Getting started Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family: Exports and CSS variables: GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif GeistSerifRegular : --font-geist-serif-regular GeistSerifSquare : --font-geist-serif-square GeistSerifTriangle : --font-geist-serif-triangle GeistSerifHeart : --font-geist-serif-heart Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular : You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font . What’s next Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start. Weights from Thin to Black The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at. Toward a text face To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight. Italics, built rule by rule We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster. More scripts and Google Fonts Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch. One family With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together. Download Geist Serif and start building. Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible. None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes. Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you. Read more

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
raw_summary: Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache , you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations. Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate. Why we built Runtime Cache Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache . Unlike CDN caching , which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor. We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions . Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps. Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote' , which caches function and component outputs. How Runtime Cache works The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data. Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys. On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy. Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale. For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog . When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually. The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN , distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds. Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions. What we’ve shipped Faster reads during traffic bursts Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available. We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh. We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped. More storage and fewer evictions We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day. More visibility into cache behavior We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability . These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read. Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with. If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache , nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage. Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing . New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance. See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes. Read more

title: Evaluating New LinkedIn Labor Market Tightness Indicators
raw_summary: Measures of labor market tightness (LMT) describe how difficult it is for firms to find workers. The labor market is considered tight if there are few job seekers available relative to job openings, implying stronger wage pressures as employers compete for scarce job seekers. Thus, good measures of LMT are important for predicting wage inflation and calibrating monetary policy. Recently, the hiring platform LinkedIn began producing three innovative LMT measures based on its user data. In this post, we use public data from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) to evaluate the ability of these novel measures to predict wage and price inflation relative to existing LMT measures, finding that one stands out as particularly useful and timely.

title: FEDS Paper: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
raw_summary: Aditya Aladangady , Ricardo Duque Gabriel , and Carlo Wix We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely track traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level, capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level, and reproducing the impulse response of official consumption measures to identified monetary policy shocks. We then use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find suggestive evidence that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.

title: Capital One at EMNLP 2026 in Budapest

Advancing natural language processing through multi-sector research Natural language processing (NLP) forms the backbone of modern agentic systems, document intelligence and enterprise artificial intelligence applications. Capital One researchers, in collaboration with our academic partners, are presenting 16 accepted papers at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026), taking place in Budapest, Hungary, October 24–29. These research papers highlight ongoing investments in foundational AI/ML science, robust red-teaming, graph-encoded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), intent resolution and trustworthy evaluation techniques. Multi-sector collaboration accelerates the transition of foundational NLP innovations into secure, reliable enterprise systems. By co-authoring several of these papers with university partners including the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Southern California and UNC Chapel Hill, Capital One contributes to open science while addressing complex technical challenges at scale. Highlighted EMNLP 2026 research papers Papers on robustness, red-teaming and model safety: FinRT: Distilling adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators in consumer finance Rikhiya Ghosh, Himanshu Kumar, Sriram Venkatapathy, Sahil Wadhwa, Alexandre Day, Andy Luo, Pranab Mohanty Large language models remain susceptible to adversarial prompts that induce policy-violating behavior in regulated financial contexts. This work introduces FinRT, a framework that distills adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators, significantly improving attack detection and safety verification under fixed generation budgets. MEMGUARD: Preventing memory contamination in long-term memory-augmented large language models Hyeonjeong Ha, William Campbell, Yue Wu (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Long-term memory integration introduces risks of memory contamination in conversational agents. The authors present MEMGUARD, a defense system designed to inspect, isolate and neutralize untrusted external inputs before they corrupt long-term memory stores. Validity-aware jailbreak evaluation for large language models Qilong Wu, Sahil Wadhwa, Pranab Mohanty, Giri Iyengar (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Standard jailbreak evaluations frequently misclassify unviable prompts as successful security breaches. This paper establishes a validity-aware benchmark framework that rigorously validates execution success to ensure accurate safety measurements across frontier language models. Papers on advanced retrieval, graph encoding and intent resolution: CAGE: Coherence-aware graph encoding for retrieval-augmented generation Tong Qi, Jingyu Wu, Youbing Yin, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Traditional vector-based retrieval systems often retrieve relevant to query but collectively incoherent text chunks. CAGE introduces a graph-encoding framework that structures retrieved passages into directed heterogeneous graphs to preserve context relevance, factual consistency and cross-chunk coherence. SPARC-RAG: Adaptive sequential–parallel scaling with context management for retrieval-augmented generation Yuxin Yang, Nima Chitsazan, Yash Govilkar, Akasha Tigalappanavara, Sambit Sahu, Shixiong Zhang (academic partnership with University of Southern California) Naive inference-time scaling in RAG causes context contamination and diminishing returns during complex reasoning. SPARC-RAG coordinates sequential refinement and parallel exploration via unified context management, improving accuracy at lower inference cost. Probing ambiguity: Adversarial intent resolution for robust text-to-SQL Youbing Yin, Xujun Peng, Muhammad Uddin, Erin Babinsky, Daben Liu, Anoop Kumar Natural language database queries frequently contain implicit ambiguities that yield multiple SQL query translations. This paper presents Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR), a multi-agent framework that actively probes for ambiguity, verifies execution differences and generates targeted clarification. The framework remains effective even when only the database schema, not the underlying data is exposed to the LLM. Papers on LLM evaluation, debiasing and benchmarking: The judge can debias itself: Awareness and self debiasing for reliable LLM-as-a-judge Youbing Yin, Jingyu Wu, Anoop Kumar, Scott Novotney, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Automated LLM-as-a-judge frameworks inherit systematic biases when evaluating output quality. The researchers introduce new benchmarks for additional bias types and demonstrate that self-debiasing strategies can effectively help detect and calibrate their own biases. title: Brits nearly twice as likely to spot pressure tactics in horror films as investment red flags
raw_summary: Investors are almost twice as likely to recognise pressure tactics in a horror film as they are when those tactics are used to promote an investment opportunity, new FCA data suggests. A survey of UK 18 to 40-year-olds who own or are considering investments found 65% spotted ‘this is your only chance’ as a classic horror warning sign. But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out. The pattern also holds for other pressure tactics. While 59% recognised countdowns like the ticking clock in 'Saw' as a tactic designed to make characters act rashly, just 5% said they would be suspicious of the pressure created by a rising investment price graph.Blind spots show up with novelty, too. Nearly half (47%) recognised that horror sequels often bring back familiar threats disguised as something new. Yet only 12% were similarly sceptical of a 'groundbreaking new' investment product, while 1 in 10 said being new would actually make them more likely to invest. Peer pressure and hype also influenced attitudes towards investment. While 80% recognised ‘trust me, it's fine, everyone's doing it’ as a warning sign in a horror scenario, almost 3 in 10 (29%) said excitement from friends or group chats about an investment would reassure them or make them trust the opportunity rather than doing their own research. Lucy Castledine, director of consumer investments at the FCA, said: 'Many people can spot a horror movie trap a mile off, but this survey suggests they’re far less likely to recognise the same tactics when they're used to influence investment decisions. Hype, urgency and fear of missing out can all influence how people invest, so before acting on an opportunity, do your research and make sure it's right for you.'The FCA's InvestSmart campaign helps consumers make more informed investment decisions. Its Hype Type Revealer helps people understand what may influence their decisions and how to avoid being drawn in by investment hype.Note to editors Research conducted by Attest on behalf of the FCA. Fieldwork conducted on 9 October 2026. The sample comprised 666 respondents based in the UK, and was open to all adults across the 18 to 40 age range. All participants either currently own investments or would consider buying investments in the next 12 months.Additional findings from the research include:Around half of respondents hold a stocks and shares ISA.1 in 4 own cryptocurrency.Nearly 1 in 10 own NFTs.Initial testing of the Hype Type Revealer with more than 600 retail investors found its training intervention reduced high-risk investment decisions by 34.9%, even 7 days later.

title: What does 'fair value' look like in practice? Three years into the Consumer Duty, here’s what we’ve learned.
raw_summary: Fair value is a simple yet important principle at the heart of the Consumer Duty: the price customers pay should be reasonable, relative to the benefits they get. But applying that principle in practice requires judgement.Three years into the Consumer Duty, we’re seeing clear differences between firms that have embedded fair value into their approach and those that still need to strengthen their assessments, evidence and monitoring.We recently reviewed how firms across the consumer finance market assess, evidence and monitor fair value. We also carried out focused work on fees and charges across a range of credit products, and supervisory work on consumer hire and third-party ownership agreements for home energy infrastructure.Many firms are getting it right, building fair value into how they design, price and monitor their products. Others are missing things that, in hindsight, could have been avoidable. Where firms fell short, a recurring issue was the evidence supporting their conclusions.Here are 3 areas that separated the 2, and questions firms can use to challenge their approach to assessing and monitoring fair value.Does your evidence actually tell you something, or just describe your product?Across the firms and products we reviewed, stronger fair value assessments showed a clear, evidenced relationship between what customers paid and the benefits they could reasonably expect to receive. One credit card provider, for example, quantified the cashback, foreign exchange savings and other account benefits customers received, and set these directly against the fees and interest they paid. That gave them a clear evidence base for their fair value conclusion, not just a description of the product's features.Weaker assessments tended to rely on assumptions rather than actual customer data. Some had relevant evidence, but it was scattered across different documents and never brought together into a coherent picture. This made it hard for anyone, including us, to see how firms had reached their conclusions.Are you assessing fair value for different customer groups?Fair value isn't one-size-fits-all. Firms showing an understanding of that nuance segmented their customers by factors such as credit risk, product usage, distribution channel and characteristics of vulnerability, and assessed fair value across the resulting groups. Some firms also assessed fair value across different pricing groups, including APR bands and risk-based pricing groups, to understand whether customers paying different prices continued to receive fair value. Other firms treated their whole target market as a single, homogeneous group when testing fair value. This made it difficult to spot if some customers were quietly paying more, or getting less, than others, which is exactly the kind of thing a fair value assessment is supposed to identify.If customers can't picture the real cost, does the price even matter?Fair value also needs to be considered alongside customer understanding. Even a well-designed, fairly priced product can fall short if customers don't understand what they're signing up to. Some firms tested comprehension directly, including one that proactively contacted customers incurring certain charges to check they understood how and when those charges applied. This gave the firm evidence about whether customers understood the charges, rather than relying only on the existence or readability of disclosures.We also looked at consumer hire agreements for home energy equipment, where some promotions used 'pay as you save' claims that could lead customers to believe that savings or affordability were guaranteed. Those outcomes depended on factors such as equipment performance, changes in customers’ circumstances and future energy prices over agreements lasting up to 25 years. Firms should make these clear and avoid creating the impression that savings or affordability are assured.What this means for your firm Use these findings to challenge your approach to assessing and monitoring fair value. Ask:Does your evidence tell you something meaningful about customer outcomes, or does it simply describe your product?Does your target market behave as one group once you look closely?Can customers understand the total price they might pay and the financial commitment they are entering into?A common feature of stronger approaches was that firms supported their conclusions with evidence rather than relying on assumptions.The good news is that this doesn’t need to always require complex modelling or new data. Smaller firms may be able to draw on information they already hold, including complaints, arrears, customer feedback and product usage.If there's one thing to take from this, it's to show your working: what your evidence shows, how it supports your conclusion, what you'd do if it didn't.We expect firms to read the full findings. They also cover how firms assessed total price and benefits, used competitor benchmarking, and used controls to reduce the risk of foreseeable harm from fees and charges, including the home energy sector examples we touched on above.We'll keep monitoring this area through our supervisory work and will continue sharing what we learn as our understanding develops.

title: FCA stops HTX's crypto promotions
raw_summary: The FCA has secured High Court undertakings to ensure that HTX (formerly Huobi), a global crypto exchange, will not knowingly promote cryptoasset services unlawfully to UK consumers. The FCA took legal action against HTX in October 2025 for breaking UK financial promotion rules. HTX had failed repeatedly to engage with the FCA. Following the commencement of proceedings, HTX took steps to exit the UK. The FCA and Huobi Global S.A. have now reached a settlement in the case. HTX is no longer active in the UK. Consumers can no longer make deposits, and new UK users cannot sign up to the platform. HTX will not target, solicit or actively seek to engage UK consumers.UK users of HTX should read the information published on HTX's website about the availability of its services in the UK and the arrangements for withdrawing any residual assets.Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said: 'Crypto firms should be under no illusion: being based overseas does not put them beyond the reach of UK law. Our action means HTX is leaving the UK and can no longer target UK consumers. The message to other firms is clear: follow the rules or face the consequences.'Consumers should check a firm's permissions using the FCA Firm Checker and remember that cryptoassets are high-risk investments.Notes to editorsRead details of the proceedings and relevant court documents. Huobi Global S.A. is the first defendant in the proceedings.View the court order (PDF) containing the undertakings. Huobi Global's undertakings to the court include that it will not knowingly, directly or indirectly, communicate or cause to be communicated a financial promotion in contravention of section 21 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. This covers the HTX website, software applications and social media platforms.The proceedings were commenced in the Business and Property Division of the High Court on 21 October 2025.The FCA publicly announced its enforcement action on 10 February 2026. The terms of the settlement are confidential. The settlement does not constitute an admission of liability or wrongdoing by Huobi Global or any other person or entity.Crypto is a high-risk investment and remains largely unregulated in the UK, except for anti-money laundering and financial promotions until October 2027. Use the FCA Firm Checker to check a firm’s permissions.

title: Defence SMEs need banking services that work
raw_summary: The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusionThe current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.Defence is not one-size-fits-allThere is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.Better information leads to better decisionsAnother theme that stood out was the importance of data.Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:Are applications taking longer than expected?Are decisions being applied consistently?Do governance processes reflect actual risk?Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.Getting the balance rightOur work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.Read our findings.

title: FCA calls on private market firms to manage conflicts of interest in line with rapid growth
raw_summary: Private market firms vary in how well they identify and manage conflicts of interest, according to an FCA review. Private markets refer to investments in assets, companies, or debt not listed or traded on public exchanges. They’ve grown significantly in recent years, and the UK is a leading international centre. Private markets play an increasingly important role in providing capital to businesses and opportunities for returns to investors. Private markets can give rise to conflicts that differ from those in public markets, and effective disclosure is important to enable investors to assess whether their interests are being protected.The FCA found examples of good practice by firms across private equity, private credit and real estate asset classes. These included strong governance arrangements, effective oversight and independent challenge. It also identified some areas where firms could strengthen governance, oversight and conflicts management arrangements to support fair investor outcomes.As private markets grow and business models become more complex, the FCA found that some firms were failing to identify conflicts adequately or keep their controls up to date. Recurring weaknesses were identified in areas including cross-fund transfers and multi-party transactions, gifts and entertainment, and information barriers.The FCA expects firms to be able to identify, record, manage and disclose conflicts effectively, and demonstrate that investors are being treated fairly, particularly in areas where investors place significant reliance on firms' judgement, governance and controls.Michelle Beck, director of wholesale buy-side at the FCA, said: 'Firms need to ensure their management of conflicts of interest keeps pace with growth in their size and complexity. We found good practice across the sector, but standards varied considerably. We want to encourage confidence in the UK’s private markets. Firms should act on our findings and identify where they can strengthen controls.'Although not part of this review, the FCA is examining governance and conflicts concerns relating to the use of private credit to fund consumer litigation claims, including significant risks of harm to investors, consumers and markets.Notes to editorsConflicts of interest and fair customer treatment in private markets.The review examined how firms identify, manage, mitigate and disclose conflicts of interest across private equity, private credit and real estate markets.The report includes examples of both good practice and areas where firms could strengthen arrangements.The review forms part of the FCA's wider supervisory focus on private markets and investor outcomes.

title: Beyond borders: Regulating the risks we share
raw_summary: Speech by Ashley Alder, FCA Chair, at the Michael D. Gill Lecture on International Financial Regulatory Understanding and Cooperation. I wasn’t fortunate enough to work as closely with Mike as many of you in this room.But I knew him well enough during my time with the IOSCO board to appreciate someone who was kind and unassuming, whilst being absolutely determined to make lives better through his work.He personified the very best attributes of dedicated public service.In his 2024 lecture Andrew Bailey described Mike as a passionate internationalist, and reflected on what this meant for the UK after the Brexit referendum.Two years on, the values that Mike championed are even more on point.Mike understood implicitly that relationships between regulators are about so much more than institutional goodwill – they depend on trust, candour and constructive practical action.That’s an aspect of his legacy that is just as relevant – perhaps even more so – today.In an increasingly interconnected global financial system, no institution can see the whole picture on its own.Success depends not only on what each regulator does individually, but on what we can see, understand, test, and address together.

title: FCA restricts 6 firms following concerns over anti-money laundering controls
raw_summary: Restrictions have been placed on 6 unregulated lenders, known as Annex 1 firms, after the FCA raised concerns about their anti-money laundering policies, controls and procedures while assessing their applications. The restrictions were imposed by the FCA on each firm’s request and limit their ability to take on new customers or do new business with existing customers, including extending existing credit.This action forms part of the FCA’s enhanced oversight of Annex 1 firms. These firms operate in sectors that can present a heightened risk of money laundering and other financial crime and are required to register with the FCA for supervision under the Money Laundering Regulations. They are not authorised or subject to wider FCA regulation.The FCA has previously warned Annex 1 firms that they will be subject to increased scrutiny. They must be able to demonstrate they understand the financial crime risks they face and have effective systems and controls in place to manage those risks, or face action.More widely, the FCA is assessing responses to an information request sent to around 900 registered Annex 1 firms to identify and disrupt financial crime risks and determine where further action is needed.The FCA has also reminded regulated firms that, when dealing with Annex 1 firms, they must carry out due diligence to understand the firm’s business, in accordance with legislative requirements. This includes seeking direct confirmation from the firm of its registration status, conducting independent checks of the information it provides, and understanding and managing any risks.Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is not a substitute for regulated firms carrying out their own appropriate due diligence.Steve Smart, executive director lead for fighting financial crime at the FCA, said: 'We have warned Annex 1 firms that they face increased scrutiny. They must demonstrate they can manage the money laundering risks they face. Where they cannot satisfy us, we will intervene.'Notes to editorsVoluntary restrictions were imposed on Kingscrown Finance Ltd on 21 April 2026, with further voluntary restrictions imposed on 25 September 2026. The further restrictions limit how Kingscrown may receive payments from existing customers and require an orderly wind-down of its existing loan book.On 7 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on MOMSB Ltd and Momentus Capital Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements subject to limited exceptions, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 9 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Grosvenor Funding Ltd and Grosvenor Funding (North West) Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 15 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Abbital Ltd. The restrictions specify the circumstances in which Abbital may take on new customers, enter into new lending arrangements or accept payments from existing customers. They also require an independent review of Abbital’s anti-money laundering systems and controls.Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA's strategic priorities.

title: Market integrity in a digital age

title: Reshaping regulation, deliberately
raw_summary: Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026. Reform: more than writing rulesIn this sector, we’re just past peak rule making. The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.But we’re not done yet.We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.It takes a strategic approach. One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions.And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.We’ve introduced targeted support.And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.We’re already seeing real progress.Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.But it’s well worth it.

title: Former chief executive banned after misconduct led to £4m losses in high-risk investments
raw_summary: The FCA has banned Jeffrey Dawkins, the former chief executive of Vector Wealth Ltd, after he dishonestly acted as a front for a disqualified director using the company to sell high-risk bonds. Mr Dawkins has also been fined nearly £270,000.In 2019, Mr Dawkins sold Vector Wealth to a disqualified director who described himself as CEO and wanted to use Vector Wealth’s FCA-authorised status to sell mini-bonds.Mr Dawkins told the FCA he was still in charge, but the new “CEO” was really running the firm. This deception allowed the disqualified director to promote mini-bonds using the legitimacy of the firm to make them appear safer than they were.The disqualified director and Kadir Kanizi, a former senior manager at Vector Wealth, promoted the bonds but investors were not properly warned about the risks.Investors put in £105,000 on average, with one investing £1.1 million. Before seeing the marketing material, they had to confirm they were high net worth or sophisticated investors. Investors are expected to lose about £4 million.The FCA has banned Mr Kanizi from senior management roles. He was fined for failing to make sure consumers were properly warned about the risks.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said, 'Jeffrey Dawkins acted as a front man for a banned director, helping high-risk investments look safer than they were.'Mr Dawkins and Mr Kanizi allowed misleading promotions to draw in investors, many of whom now face significant losses. Mini-bonds and similar investments are very high risk, and people should be extremely cautious.'The FCA has warned about the risks of investing in mini-bonds and loan notes. A loan note or mini-bond usually involves lending money to a company for a set period in return for interest. If that company fails, consumers could lose every penny.Consumers need to be alert to the risk of harm and protect themselves using the tools available, like the FCA Firm Checker.Notes to editorsRead the final notices for Jeffrey Dawkins and Kadir Kanizi.There is statutory obligation to report the change in control of authorised firms.Vector Wealth Limited was formed as Fifth Quarter Asset Management (UK) Limited on 23 March 2012. Mr Dawkins held authorised positions at the firm from 5 March 2013. Vector Wealth’s authorisation ended on 28 January 2025.Mr Kanizi was appointed as a director on 22 September 2020 and was approved by the FCA on 6 September 2021.The disqualified director was banned from acting as a company director for 12 years in August 2014.The penalty in respect of Mr Dawkins includes a multiplier to reflect the seriousness of the conduct. It also includes an uplift for failing to cooperate with the FCA’s investigation. The full calculation is set out at section 6 of the Final Notice. Mr Dawkins has also been ordered to pay £57,298 plus interest (£68,257) of the proceeds he received from selling Vector Wealth and continuing to act as its director and approved person.The FCA has calculated that Kadir Kanizi should have been fined £80,096 but it reduced the penalty to £20,000 after he demonstrated that it would cause serious financial hardship. In the interest of maximising the funds available to be distributed to investors, the FCA agreed not to enforce the penalty if the same amount was made available by Mr Kanizi to Vector Wealth’s liquidators. He has also agreed to complete consumer duty training before taking up any future role in financial services.Investors who bought bonds through Vector Wealth should contact the firm’s liquidator and check the FCA website for updates.The FCA has investigated the matters that fall within its remit. The FCA may share relevant information with other law enforcement agencies where appropriate. Confirming or comment on individual referrals could risk affecting ongoing investigations.The FCA now actively removes the unutilised permissions of firms. Historically firms were expected to voluntarily request cancellation of unused permissions.The FCA permanently banned the marketing of speculative illiquid securities, including mini-bonds and loan notes, to retail investors from 1 January 2021.Anyone approached about loan notes, mini-bonds or similar high-risk investments should stop and check before investing, especially where adverts promise big, fixed returns or make the investment look simple and safe. Use the FCA’s Firm Checker and Warning List before handing over any money.

title: Three arrests in major FCA operation against criminal insider dealing ring
raw_summary: The FCA has conducted a major operation to disrupt a suspected organised criminal group for engaging in insider dealing and money laundering. On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.More than 30 mobile phones, laptops and tablets were seized in searches conducted by FCA investigators.All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'Insider dealing is a serious threat to the integrity of our markets. Working with partners, we will continue to use all the powers at our disposal to crack down on serious and organised crime groups engaged in market abuse.'In 2025/26, the FCA secured 4 insider dealing convictions, with 2 resulting in record sentences totalling 11 years of imprisonment. Twelve people were fined a total of £1.77m for insider dealing, market manipulation and making misleading statements.Notes to editorsThe FCA cannot comment further at this time but will provide more details when appropriate.Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.If you have information concerning insider dealing you can contact the FCA by phone on 0800 111 6768 or by using the FCA’s reporting form. Information can be passed confidentially.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

title: Two plead guilty after clients lose £2m in fraud case
raw_summary: Two people who worked at financial advice firms have pleaded guilty to fraud after 4 clients lost £2m. Kerry Nelson, the director of Nexus Independent Financial Advisers Limited and Nexus Investment Managers Limited, and Jacqueline Stephens, the firms' business operations manager, admitted all charges brought by the FCA at Portsmouth Crown Court.They admitted defrauding clients between January 2019 and January 2023 and using false documents as part of the fraud. Nelson has also admitted a money laundering offence after money was withdrawn from the firms, which she used to fund her extravagant lifestyle.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'This was a serious breach of trust. Nelson and Stephens caused significant losses to clients who relied on them. We will continue to act where people exploit clients for their own gain.'Nelson and Stephens will be sentenced at Portsmouth Crown Court on 10 December 2026. The FCA will seek confiscation proceedings to deprive Kerry Nelson of any financial benefit from her criminal conduct.Notes to editorsThe FCA started criminal proceedings against Kerry Nelson and Jacqueline Stephens in February 2025. For more details see, FCA charges two individuals with multiple fraud charges. They pleaded guilty at Portsmouth Crown Court on 12 October 2026.Fraud by abuse of position is an offence under sections 1 and 4 of the Fraud Act 2006.Using a false instrument is an offence under section 3 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981.Converting or transferring criminal property is an offence under section 327(1) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Confiscation proceedings will be pursued under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Nexus IFA and Nexus IM were authorised by the FCA. Nexus IFA had permissions to provide investment, mortgage and pension advice and Nexus IM to provide discretionary fund management services. Neither firm was permitted to hold or control client money.On 25 January 2023, the FCA imposed restrictions preventing both firms from carrying on regulated activity and from reducing the value of the assets they held. The High Court placed both firms into administration on 26 January 2023.

title: How to Make Artificial Intelligence More Environmentally Sustainable
raw_summary: IT is responsible for about 2 - 4% of all global emissions, and electricity use at Microsoft and Google has climbed because of AI, according to their own reports. Sustainability ought to be a top-level architectural concern. Some recommendations are: use pre-built and smaller models, run compute where low-carbon electricity is abundant, and train on renewable energy. By Ben Linders
